content: HIV testing services (HTS) can be strategically implemented in specific health facilities to address the needs of populations or areas with high HIV prevalence or unmet testing demands. This approach is particularly effective for reaching individuals at high risk of HIV or those with undiagnosed infections, such as members of key populations, sexual and social networks with ongoing HIV transmission risk, partners, family members, peers, or social contacts of people living with HIV. Additionally, underserved groups, such as men, adolescents in high HIV burden settings, and vulnerable populations like migrant workers, may benefit from targeted HTS depending on the local context. HTS can also be focused on specific geographic areas or settings with high HIV burden and ongoing transmission, such as transport hubs, border crossings, or urban locales where key populations work or reside. Community-based testing, mobile outreach, home-based testing, and the distribution of HIV self-testing (HIVST) kits in workplaces, schools, and other venues can be effective in areas with low testing coverage and high HIV prevalence or incidence. Geographic prioritization can help scale up new HTS approaches gradually, increasing coverage as resources become available. Indicator condition-guided HTS involves offering testing to individuals presenting with clinical conditions indicative of HIV infection, such as cervical or anal cancer/dysplasia, herpes zoster, or unexplained fever. This method has been successfully implemented in routine healthcare settings in Europe, supported by WHO region-specific guidance. Data from 20 low HIV burden European countries showed a 3% HIV positivity rate when testing was offered to individuals with indicator conditions. Partner services, including voluntary provider-assisted referral, should be offered to all people living with HIV to reach their sexual or drug-injecting partners and biological children with unknown HIV status. This approach ensures comprehensive care and prevention. Retesting for HIV-negative individuals or those with unknown status serves two main purposes: monitoring the effectiveness of HIV prevention interventions and identifying new infections early when prevention efforts fail. Most people with a negative HIV test do not require retesting unless they report recent or ongoing HIV risk exposure. In low HIV burden settings, a single lifetime test is sufficient for most individuals without ongoing risk. Annual retesting is recommended for sexually active individuals in high HIV burden settings and those with ongoing HIV-related risks, such as key populations (e.g., men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals) and individuals with HIV-positive partners who are not virally suppressed. Retesting may also be warranted for individuals presenting with sexually transmitted infections (STIs), viral hepatitis, tuberculosis (TB), or clinical conditions indicative of HIV. More frequent retesting (every 3–6 months) may be necessary for individuals with higher risk factors, such as those taking pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) or members of key populations presenting with an STI. Pregnant and breastfeeding women face increased HIV acquisition risk, particularly in high HIV burden settings or if they have HIV-positive partners. All pregnant women should be offered testing for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) early in pregnancy, ideally at the first antenatal care (ANC) visit. In high HIV burden settings, retesting in late pregnancy (third trimester) is advised for women with unknown or negative HIV status. If initial or retesting is missed, catch-up testing is necessary. Postpartum retesting can be considered for women from key populations or those with HIV-positive partners who are not virally suppressed. Mathematical modeling and cost-effectiveness analyses indicate that maternal HIV retesting during pregnancy is cost-effective in high HIV burden countries, such as Kenya and South Africa, but not in low burden settings like Colombia or Ukraine. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) at the first ANC visit are cost-saving in both high and low burden settings. For individuals with HIV who are not on antiretroviral therapy (ART) or receiving other HIV care, retesting can serve as a pathway to re-engage in care. This includes those diagnosed in the pre-ART era or individuals who started ART but disengaged from care. Efforts should focus on effective linkage to ART for these individuals. Validated screening tools or questionnaires can help identify individuals who would benefit from HTS in settings where testing is not routinely offered or to improve efficiency in settings with low positivity rates. However, careful consideration is needed to ensure these tools do not deter individuals from testing due to confidentiality concerns or miss those at high risk. Retesting strategies should be tailored to the local HIV epidemiology, resource availability, and population needs to optimize HTS delivery effectively.
